tour.title: Shinjuku to Shibuya: The Modern City After Dark
tour.summary: A shrine in a donated forest, the two districts that invented Japanese youth fashion, a crossing that moves three thousand people on one green light, a station used by three million a day, and a black-market alley — finishing 202 metres up, free.
tour.overviewText:
Tokyo is a city of fourteen million where you can walk almost anywhere at midnight and, statistically, nothing will happen to you — and this walk explains how, and at what price.

The story starts with the man the first stop enshrines. Emperor Meiji (1852–1912) reigned through the Meiji Restoration of 1868 — the revolution that ended two and a half centuries of Tokugawa shogunate rule, moved the capital from Kyoto, renamed the city Tokyo, eastern capital, and drove Japan from a closed agrarian country to industrial power in a generation. After his death the nation built him a shrine. Shinto is Japan's indigenous religion; a shrine is the dwelling of a kami — not a god in the Western sense but a sacred presence — and here the kami are Meiji and his wife Empress Shōken — venerated, not buried, here. The shrine is younger than it looks: dedicated in 1920, destroyed in the 1945 air raids, rebuilt by public donation in 1958. Around it stands a seventy-hectare forest of roughly a hundred thousand trees donated from every corner of Japan, planted by volunteers, wholly artificial, and designed by forestry experts to renew itself over a century. Ten minutes in, the city is gone; that is engineering.

Then the city that grew around it. Tokyo was emptied twice — 1923 earthquake, 1945 bombing — and rebuilt twice. The districts here are that project's soft power. Harajuku and Shibuya were teenage inventions: street fashion, then pop, then the aesthetic the world buys as kawaii, cute pushed to the point of costume. Omotesandō let luxury brands turn a 1919 avenue into an open-air architecture exhibition. Shinjuku is the other face: government, the world's busiest railway station, and the drinking alleys born of the black market in the ashes of 1945.

That calm is not luck. Handguns are effectively banned; some six thousand kōban — neighbourhood police posts that give directions and log lost wallets — spread community policing everywhere; police clear almost every homicide they attend. The counterweight: a safe street is not a well society. Japan loses roughly twenty thousand people a year to suicide, and part of the night economy you pass through exists for people who are otherwise alone.

The route runs one way and stays level: mid-afternoon in the forest at Meiji Jingū, Harajuku's fashion lane, the zelkova avenue of Omotesandō, then down into Shibuya for the crossing and Hachikō. Measured end to end it is 8.6 kilometres and two hours of walking, but one leg is ridden: Shibuya to Shinjuku, a five-minute train against 4.2 kilometres and fifty-nine minutes on foot. On foot you actually cover about 4.4 kilometres. Then the alley, dinner at a counter, and the free observatory.

Practicals, February 2027. Start about 14:30: Meiji Jingū closes at sunset, 16:50 in February, so the shrine comes first; dusk at 17:20 puts you at the crossing in the dark and in Shinjuku by 19:00. Nothing charges admission except the shrine's inner garden (¥500), its museum (¥1,000) and Shibuya Sky (¥2,700). The yen (¥) is the currency, alley counters are cash-only, and a Suica or Pasmo IC card covers the train hop. Verify every hour and price at the gate.

Eat standing in an alley, drink nothing on the Shibuya kerb after six, and look up.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Level and gently sloping pavements, the shrine's gravel approach, and one train ride in the middle. The shrine path is loose gravel; the alley lane is narrow and its counters are tight; the observatory lift is step-free from the first floor.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start about 14:30 in February: Meiji Jingū shuts at 16:50, and you want Harajuku while it is still light, Omotesandō at dusk, the Shibuya crossing after dark, and an alley counter around 19:00. The observatory's south deck takes visitors until 21:30, so leave the eating to the alley and the view to last. Weekday evenings are busiest at the crossing; Sunday afternoons are busiest in Harajuku.

stops.name: Meiji Jingū: Shrine and Forest
stops.narration:
Bow slightly as you pass under the torii — the tall, unpainted wooden gate that marks the boundary between ordinary ground and sacred ground. This is the Ōtorii, the shrine's main gate, and it has a biography: the first version was cut in 1920 from a 1,200-year-old cypress on Alishan mountain in Taiwan, then a Japanese territory; lightning broke it apart in 1966, and the gate standing now was cut from a 1,500-year-old Japanese cypress. Walk on one side of the gravel path, not down the middle — the centre is left for the kami — and stop at the stone water basin, the temizuya, where you rinse your left hand, then your right, then your mouth, always with water poured from the ladle rather than with your mouth at the spout.

You are walking towards a kami. Shinto, Japan's indigenous religion, holds that sacred presence is everywhere — in mountains, waterfalls, old trees — and a shrine is a dwelling built for one of them and a place to ask it for things. Meiji Jingū enshrines Emperor Meiji (1852–1912) and his wife Empress Shōken (1850–1914). Meiji is the emperor of the Meiji Restoration: in 1868 his court ended the shogunate's rule, moved the capital from Kyoto to Edo and renamed it Tokyo, eastern capital, and within forty years Japan had railways, conscription, a parliament and an empire. He is not buried here; his tomb is in Kyoto. He is venerated here, and the shrine was a national project after his death — funded by donations, timber sent from every prefecture including the then-colonies of Taiwan and Korea, built largely with volunteer youth labour, and dedicated on 3 November 1920. Until 1946 it ranked among the kanpei-taisha, the state-supported shrines; then Japan's postwar constitution separated religion from government, and Meiji Jingū has paid its own way ever since.

That is the building. The forest is the engineering. Seventy hectares were planted — roughly a hundred thousand trees donated from all over Japan, about 365 species, set out between 1915 and the mid-1920s on what had been bare hillside and meadow. The aim was not a park but a forest that would look after itself: mostly evergreens, planted densely, designed by forestry experts to need no human tending once established, on a plan that ran a hundred years ahead. It is entirely artificial and now reads as wild. In 1945 American firebombs destroyed the shrine buildings; the forest survived untouched, and the city rebuilt the shrine in 1958 with public money.

Three things before you go. At the main hall the custom is two bows, two claps, one bow, a coin in the offering box first. The stacked sake barrels and wine barrels along the approach are offerings from brewers and wineries to the kami. And the shrine is free, open from sunrise to sunset — in February 6:20 to 16:50, so verify the day's hours and come with time in hand. The Inner Garden, which holds the iris beds and Kiyomasa's Well, costs around ¥500, the yen being Japan's currency, and shuts at 16:00 in winter; the museum by Kengo Kuma, ¥1,000, closes at 16:30 and on Thursdays between exhibitions. Then take the south approach down to Harajuku.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The shrine, forest and grounds are free — no ticket, no gate. Optional extras: the Inner Garden is around ¥500 and the Meiji Jingu Museum around ¥1,000. Verify both at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Open every day from sunrise to sunset. In February roughly 6:20 to 16:50; hours lengthen and shorten month by month, so check the official table for your date rather than trusting a sign. The Inner Garden closes at 16:00 in winter, the museum at 16:30.
stops.accessibility: The approach is wide, level compacted gravel — manageable with a stick or a wheelchair, though the surface is loose. The main shrine courtyard is flat with a few shallow steps at the gate buildings. The Inner Garden has gravel paths and some inclines.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the Ōtorii as you pass under it rather than photographing it from the front — the gate was cut from a living tree of about 1,500 years and the trunk's curve is still visible in the pillars. Then walk the first hundred metres of the forest path in silence; that un-tended, self-seeding look is the whole design brief.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the shrine by the south approach — the broad gravel avenue with the torii at its end — cross the Jingūbashi bridge, and Harajuku Station is directly ahead across the road. The entrance to Takeshita Street is on the far side of the station, a metre or two past the ticket gates. It is about 1.4 kilometres, roughly eighteen minutes at a stroll, and the last stretch through the forest is part of the stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Hyppolyte de Saint-Rambert, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Takeshita Street, Harajuku
stops.narration:
You are at the mouth of a lane about 350 metres long and four to six metres wide, sloping down from Harajuku Station to the wide road called Meiji-dōri. From 11:00 until 18:00 it is closed to vehicles and belongs entirely to pedestrians. Nearly everything on it is aimed at teenagers and the people who want to look like them, and it has worked that way for fifty years.

The name is older than the fashion. Until 1965 the low ground between the station and Meiji-dōri was a town called Takeshita-chō; the address reform of that year folded it into Jingūmae, which is why Harajuku does not exist on a modern map — it survives as the station's name and as everyone's shorthand. The street became a shopping street almost by accident. After the war this area sat beside Washington Heights, an American military housing compound on what is now Yoyogi Park, and the shops along the road sold to those families: the Kiddyland toy store, the Oriental Bazaar souvenirs. In 1957 Harajuku was made Tokyo's first fudō-chiiki, an education district — a zoning category that keeps out pachinko parlours, gambling and love hotels — and residents have used that protection ever since to stay a shopping street rather than a nightlife quarter. Then came the 1964 Tokyo Olympics: the housing compound was returned, the athletes' village and Kenzō Tange's Yoyogi gymnasium went up on it, the area filled with boutiques and cafés for visitors, and Japanese teenagers discovered the place first.

That is when this lane became the country's teenage capital. Local merchants date year one to 1974; Marion Crepes opened here in 1977 and made the crêpe this street's signature food. In 1979 came the Takenoko-zoku, the bamboo-shoot tribe — teenagers who bought bright outfits at a boutique called Takenoko and danced near Yoyogi Park — the beginning of the performance of identity that Harajuku still runs on. By 1989 there were 42 shops on Takeshita selling merchandise tied to television personalities, and 52 across Harajuku. When that faded, the street moved on to gothic lolita and hip-hop, then to the extreme decoration called kawaii — cute, pushed to the point of costume — which the artist Sebastian Masuda carried worldwide from the 1990s, while the designers who grew out of the scene moved into the backstreets known as Ura-Harajuku.

Here is the mechanism, and it is why the shop in front of you may not exist next year: this street's real business is turnover. Most storefronts hold short leases, stock is reordered by the month, and a shop that keeps its sign for thirty years is a local celebrity. The crowd is the product. Two courtesies: this lane is also a school route and a neighbourhood, and eating while walking is quietly resented; and Japan has almost no public rubbish bins, so carry the cup until you find one. If you want a photograph of somebody's outfit, ask — here, more than anywhere else in this city, people often say yes and pose.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Everything you buy is at shop prices; crêpes run to a few hundred yen. Cash and cards both work on this lane.
stops.openingHours: The street itself is open at all hours, but pedestrian-only hours are roughly 11:00 to 18:00. Most shops open around 10:00 or 11:00 and close between 19:00 and 20:00; verify on the shopfronts, since hours shift by season.
stops.accessibility: Flat, paved and closed to traffic in the middle of the day, but narrow and crowded enough that a wheelchair or a pushchair will be slow going at weekends. No steps on the lane itself.
stops.insiderTip: Ignore the first hundred metres and keep walking to the far end, where the crowd thins and the shops get more experimental. Then turn round and read the lane from the Meiji-dōri end: you can see the whole slope, the station and the forest behind it in one frame.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk the lane downhill, away from the station, and it ends at Meiji-dōri, a wide avenue with traffic. Turn right and follow Meiji-dōri south for about four hundred metres until the broad, tree-lined avenue with a planted median crosses in front of you. That is Omotesandō — turn onto it and walk a couple of minutes to the long low complex on your left, Omotesandō Hills. Roughly six hundred metres in total, eight minutes.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Syced, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Omotesandō: Zelkova Boulevard
stops.narration:
The name is a description. Omote means front; sandō means approach road. This avenue, 36 metres wide and about 1.1 kilometres long, was built by the city of Tokyo in 1919 as the ceremonial front approach to Meiji Jingū, so that the emperor's new shrine would face a boulevard instead of a lane. Stand on the median and look back towards Harajuku: you are looking straight down the axis the planners set.

What made the avenue famous are the trees and what grew between them. The zelkova — keyaki in Japanese, a sturdy elm-like broadleaf with fine, hard wood — was planted here as young trees, about 200 of them, in 1921. Most burned in the firebombing of May 1945; the avenue was replanted around 1950, and of the 163 trees standing today, eleven survived the war and are now over ninety years old. In 2020 the row was listed as a heritage of civil engineering, which is Japan's way of saying that a street can be infrastructure and be loved at the same time. Look at the road's shape while you walk: it dips through the middle because it was cut at a fixed gradient across the valley of the Shibuya river, with stone retaining walls on either side.

Then the shops, which are the real surprise. From the 1970s this was the address where Japanese youth fashion grew up — first the DC brands, short for Designer's and Character's, labels that sold a complete look rather than a single garment, worn in the 1980s by the karasu-zoku, the crow tribe, who dressed in black from collar to shoe. When that faded, the international luxury houses moved in and discovered that in Tokyo a flagship store is judged as architecture, not as retail. Prada Aoyama, a glass building the shape of a cut crystal, is by Herzog & de Meuron; Dior by SANAA; Tod's by Toyo Itō, wrapped in a concrete tracery of tree branches; Louis Vuitton by Jun Aoki. And Omotesandō Hills by Tadao Andō, finished in 2006, is a 250-metre-long complex with a spiralling interior ramp that anyone can walk for free. It replaced the Dōjunkai Aoyama Apartments, a 1927 concrete block in the Bauhaus manner — the kind of modernist housing Japan built after the 1923 earthquake — and that demolition became the country's standing argument about whether it preserves anything at all. A fragment of the old block was rebuilt inside the new building, which is either a memorial or an alibi, depending on who you ask.

That is the paradox of a designer boulevard: the buildings are permanent and the fashion is not. Rents on this avenue are among the highest in Japan, so it sells long-established brands out of young buildings, and the experiments happen in the small lanes behind you.

Practical, and then onward. Most shops open around 11:00 and shut around 20:00, cafés later, and hours move with the season, so read the doors as you go. In winter the zelkova row is strung with illuminations after dark, which is the best reason to walk this stretch rather than ride it. Keep going south-east and the avenue meets Aoyama-dōri at Omotesandō station, where the walk turns down towards Shibuya.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the avenue, and free to walk the spiral ramp inside Omotesandō Hills. Shops, cafés and museums along it charge their own prices.
stops.openingHours: The avenue is open at all hours. Most shops run roughly 11:00 to 20:00, with cafés later; winter illuminations usually switch on at dusk and run into the evening. Verify individual doors.
stops.accessibility: Wide, level pavements on both sides with a planted median and zebra crossings at the junctions; the smoothest long walk on this tour. The road dips gently in the middle. Omotesandō Hills has lifts and a spiral ramp.
stops.insiderTip: Find the eleven zelkova that survived the 1945 firebombing — they are the thickest trunks, mostly near the Omotesandō Hills end — and read the small explanatory plaque about the original planting. Then look at the crown of the row at dusk in winter, when the lights come on and the whole avenue reads as one piece of infrastructure.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow the avenue south-east to its end at Aoyama-dōri, cross, and continue south-west along Aoyama-dōri — past Aoyama Gakuin and the university hospital — until the road drops into the Shibuya valley and the crossing appears below you. It is about 1.4 kilometres, roughly eighteen minutes on foot, and the avenue you walk out is the sight. If the weather has turned, ride instead: Omotesandō station is on the Hanzōmon Line, one stop to Shibuya, about two minutes.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: gog.creator, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Shibuya Scramble Crossing and Hachikō
stops.narration:
Stand still for one full cycle and watch what the intersection does. This is a scramble crossing — you will also see it called a diagonal crossing, or sukuranburu kōsaten — which means that when the pedestrian phase opens, every vehicle movement stops at once and people cross in every direction, including straight diagonals. At an ordinary intersection pedestrians make two crossings and wait twice; the scatter pattern lets them take the shortest line in a single go, which is how one green light here can move as many as three thousand people. The whole cycle turns on a loop of roughly two minutes. A 2014 survey counted about 260,000 pedestrians on an average weekday and 390,000 on a non-working day, and other estimates put the busiest days at half a million. The crossing was inaugurated in 1973, the same year the PARCO store opened up the hill and confirmed Shibuya as young Tokyo's headquarters.

Now walk to the corner where the crowd keeps stopping to take selfies and meet Hachikō. He was a creamy-white Akita dog, born in November 1923 in Ōdate, in the far north of Honshu, and brought to Shibuya in 1924 by Hidesaburō Ueno, a professor of agriculture at Tokyo Imperial University. Every evening the dog met the professor's train. On 21 May 1925 Ueno died at his desk of a cerebral haemorrhage, and Hachikō kept coming to the station anyway — for almost ten years, until his own death on 8 March 1935. Station staff fed him; children teased him; in 1932 a newspaper piece made him a national story about chūken, the faithful dog, an idea this country takes seriously. A bronze statue by the sculptor Teru Andō was unveiled in 1934 with Hachikō present; it was melted down for munitions during the war, and in 1948 the sculptor's son Takeshi Andō recast the statue you are looking at. Ōdate has its own copy, and the university has one too. The station exit beside it is named Hachikō-guchi, the Hachikō gate, and it is this city's default meeting point.

Two things to carry away. The first is scale: Shibuya Station is used by roughly three million people a day, which makes it the second-busiest railway station in the world, after Shinjuku — the crossing is, among other things, a pressure-relief valve for a station that cannot hold its own crowd. The second is that people live here. Photographers who frame the whole intersection and let the crowd stay anonymous get the better picture and leave no resentment behind, and photographing faces in a crush is the fastest way to be asked to stop.

If you want the view from above, Shibuya Sky, the open-air deck on the roof of Shibuya Scramble Square, 230 metres up and opened in 2019, sells timed tickets — around ¥2,700 booked online, and it opens late, until about 22:30 with the last entry around 21:20. Verify both at the desk, because they move. And a rule that surprises visitors: since 2024 Shibuya ward has banned drinking alcohol on the streets around the station from 6pm to 5am, all year. The convenience-store beer on the kerb is not the local custom it used to be.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to stand at the crossing; the Hachikō statue and the streets around it cost nothing. Shibuya Sky, the rooftop deck above, is the one paid view here, around ¥2,700 online — verify at the desk.
stops.openingHours: The crossing runs 24 hours a day; the video billboards stay lit into the night. Shibuya Sky is typically open about 10:00 to 22:30 with the last entry around 21:20 — check the day's times, they change seasonally. Street drinking is banned in the district from 6pm to 5am.
stops.accessibility: Level paved streets and crossing with dropped kerbs, but the crowds are the obstacle: shoulders, buggies and wheelchairs all move slowly at peak. The Hachikō statue sits on a small plaza with railings and a step-free approach from the station's Hachikō exit.
stops.insiderTip: Do not watch one crossing and leave; watch three or four cycles from the same spot and the rhythm becomes visible — the vehicle waves, the pedestrian wave, the moment the diagonal fills with people going nowhere in particular. For the photograph, use the elevated walkways and footbridges around Shibuya Station, where the whole intersection reads as one organism.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the leg you ride, unless you want a long walk. Shibuya to Shinjuku on the Shōnan–Shinjuku or Saikyō line — both run direct without a stop between — takes about five minutes; the Yamanote line takes three stops and a little longer. On foot it is 4.2 kilometres, roughly fifty-nine minutes along busy roads, so do not stroll it. Take a JR train from Shibuya and get off at Shinjuku; from the West Exit, Omoide Yokocho begins about a minute north of the exit, tucked under the railway. A Suica or Pasmo IC card — the rechargeable transit card — makes the gates painless, and the fare is a couple of hundred yen; verify at the machine.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: David Kernan, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Omoide Yokocho (Memory Lane)
stops.narration:
The official name is Shinjuku West Exit Omoide Yokocho — Memory Lane — but this alley has been called Shonben Yokocho, Piss Alley, for most of its life, and Yakitori Yokocho, Yakitori Alley, which is the more useful name tonight. Yokocho simply means side street, and this one packs roughly eighty businesses, about sixty of them eating and drinking places, into something like two thousand square metres, in two-storey timber rows with one narrow lane down the middle.

It began in the ashes. The American bombing of 1945 destroyed almost everything around Shinjuku Station, and by 1946 the west side was burnt ground with stalls selling clothing, soap and shoes and a row of thirty or forty reed-screened food stands doing oden — the winter stew of fish cakes, tofu and daikon that is still a Japanese staple. Those stands burned, and what replaced them was a black-market arcade: a yamiichi, one of the illegal markets that fed Japanese cities in the years when almost everything was rationed and the official supply system had collapsed. Here is the mechanism that built this menu. In 1947 the police were cracking down hard on controlled goods, and flour for noodles and batter was controlled. But the offal of the cattle and pigs fed to the American occupation troops was not controlled at all. So the stalls turned to the one protein that was cheap and legal, and started grilling chicken and motsu — offal, the heart, liver, tongue and intestine — over binchōtan, the hard white charcoal made from oak. Of the sixty restaurants here today, more than half are still yakitori or motsuyaki counters. Rationing invented the taste of this street.

By about 1959 the lane reached an extraordinary three hundred shops, running from Kōshū-kaidō to Ōme-kaidō, most of them on land they did not own; the redevelopment of the new station swept them away, and the block that survives is the stretch between the West Exit Hall and Ōme-kaidō. A fire in November 1999 burned 28 of the 70 shops then standing, which is why some of the timber looks newer than the rest.

Now look up, because the skyline explains the geography. This alley sits in the shadow of Shinjuku Station, the busiest railway station in the world: by the latest published counts about three million people a day use the whole complex across its operators, and JR East alone records roughly 667,000 boardings a day — a station with well over two hundred exits and platforms for a dozen lines. West of the tracks is the skyscraper district, standing on the site of the Yodobashi Water Purification Plant, Tokyo's first modern waterworks, closed in 1965 and replaced by towers. East is Kabukichō, the country's largest entertainment quarter, named in 1948 after a kabuki theatre that was never built and now holding some three thousand bars, clubs and hotels. Those clubs and love hotels are the same night economy as this alley, only scaled up.

Practical. Most counters open from about 17:00 and fill fast; seats number five to ten, so you may wait on the lane. Prices are gentle for Tokyo — a skewer roughly ¥150 to ¥300, a beer around ¥600 — but a few shops add a small seating fee on top, so ask before you sit, and many are cash-only. Some ban photographs inside, and the lane itself is private land: if you want a picture, step to the side, frame the whole alley, and never the people at the counters.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the lane; you pay for what you eat and drink. Skewers run roughly ¥150 to ¥300 and a beer around ¥600, with a seating fee at some counters — ask before you sit, and carry cash.
stops.openingHours: The lane is open at all hours, but it is a working alley: most counters open around 17:00 and close late, some after midnight, and a few serve lunch. Individual closing days vary, so read the doors.
stops.accessibility: Narrow, level lane with uneven paving and a step or two at some doorways; the counters are high stools and tight benches. A wheelchair can pass when the alley is quiet but not when it is full, and there is no step-free route through the whole lane.
stops.insiderTip: Order motsu once, whatever it turns out to be — ask the counter what today's is — because that offal skewer is the reason this alley exists and the reason it tastes unlike the yakitori chains. And sit at a counter rather than a table if you want the conversation that comes with six seats in a room built from rationing.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the alley at its north end, cross to the station's West Exit plaza and take the elevated pedestrian deck west through Nishi-Shinjuku, past the big hotels and the Nomura Building, to the twin towers of the government building — about one kilometre, fifteen minutes, all on paving with a couple of short ramps and stairs. If stairs are a problem, ride instead: the Ōedo Line runs one stop from Shinjuku station to Tochōmae, which sits directly under the building. On the way, notice that you are crossing what was, until 1965, a reservoir complex.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: MaedaAkihiko, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building Observatory
stops.narration:
You are 202 metres up, on the 45th floor of the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building, and the entrance was free. That is the fact to hold on to. This is the city hall of the Tokyo Metropolis — the prefecture-level government that administers some fourteen million people across the twenty-three special wards, the western suburbs and two island chains far out in the Pacific. It was designed by Kenzō Tange, the architect who also gave Tokyo the Yoyogi National Gymnasium you walked past near Meiji Jingū, and it was finished in December 1990 at a cost of about ¥157 billion of public money, two towers splitting out of a single block at the 33rd floor. In boom-time Tokyo that price made it a punchline: the Tax Tower, a Babel of bureaucracy, a city hall that its architect said evoked both a Gothic cathedral and an integrated circuit. But the decks on the 45th floor were put in free, and roughly two million people a year now ride the lift up to look at their own city.

What you are looking at is a machine. Follow the glow. South-east is the dark mass of Meiji Jingū and Yoyogi Park — the forest planted by hand a century ago, where this walk began — with the gardens of Shinjuku Gyoen nearer, and then the whole basin of Tokyo, one lit field of low buildings interrupted by towers. North-east stand the Sumida river and the Tokyo Skytree, a 634-metre broadcasting mast. Straight out west on a cold clear day between December and February, Mount Fuji, 100 kilometres away and 3,776 metres high; in summer haze it is simply not there, which is why winter is the season for this window. Below you, the elevated expressway follows the line of the Kōshū-kaidō, the old mountain road out of the city, and the station under your shoulder is the busiest in the world.

Now the question this walk was built to answer: how does a place this dense stay this calm? Four mechanisms, roughly in order. Guns: handguns are effectively illegal in Japan, licences are confined to hunting and target shooting under police supervision, and the whole country records only a handful of gun deaths in most years. Police: Japan has around six thousand kōban, small neighbourhood police posts staffed by a few officers whose work is deliberately unglamorous — directions, lost property, bicycle registrations, checking on older residents — and the Tokyo force posts multilingual officers at the Kabukichō and Shibuya station boxes; the emergency number is 110. Enforcement: police here clear almost every homicide they are called to, which is itself a deterrent. And pressure: a society in which strangers are expected to notice. None of that makes Tokyo a paradise. It makes it an unusually safe street, which is a narrower achievement than it sounds. Japan loses about twenty thousand people a year to suicide, a rate high among rich countries, and much of the night economy you have walked through trades in company for people who are otherwise alone. Both things are true at once, and a tour that told you only the first would be selling you something.

Turn once before you go down. The forest you walked at the start is a dark rectangle inside the lights, and the walk you have just made is one straight line of an argument: a shrine built for a dead emperor in a forest a hundred thousand people donated, two districts that invented Japanese youth culture and sold it to the world, a crossing where three thousand strangers move on one signal, an alley that rationing built, and now the city's own bureaucracy, looking back at itself, free of charge.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Both observation decks are free — no ticket, no booking. There is a café and a gift shop upstairs if you want to spend something.
stops.openingHours: The decks are free and unbookable, but the two towers keep different hours. The South deck admits visitors roughly 9:30 to 21:30; the North deck closes at 17:30, and stays open to 22:00 on days when the South deck is shut. The South deck closes on the first and third Tuesdays, the North on the second and fourth Mondays — when a holiday falls on those days the closure moves to the next working day — and both shut over the New Year period and on building inspection days. Verify the day's schedule at the desk or on the official page before you climb.
stops.accessibility: Step-free from the First Building's front entrance on the ground floor: a dedicated lift runs to the 45th floor in about a minute, and the decks are flat with seating, shops and toilets. Ask the security staff if you need the in-building lifts instead of the outside approach.
stops.insiderTip: Go up about half an hour before you mean to leave and find the south-west corner: on a clear February evening you get Fuji's silhouette against the last of the light on one side and the whole basin switching on, street by street, on the other. Tripods are not allowed, so brace on the rail.
stops.nextStopDirections: That is the end of the walk. Tochōmae station on the Ōedo Line is directly beneath the building, one stop from Shinjuku station's Ōedo platform, and Shinjuku Station is about fifteen minutes back east on foot along the same west-exit deck if you would rather walk off dinner. Taxis wait at the front entrance. If you still want a drink, Golden Gai's six lanes of two-hundred-odd tiny bars are ten minutes north-east of Shinjuku's east exit — remember that those lanes are private roads where photographing the street is banned without permission, that most bars only open around 21:00 or 22:00, and that many charge a seating fee, so ask before you sit. Otherwise: you have walked from a deified emperor's forest to the 45th floor of his city's government. Sleep well.
